{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (limb-onset, early stage)", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA) Type 3 (Kugelberg-Welander)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Multifocal Motor Neuropathy with Conduction Block", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Hereditary Motor and Sensory Neuropathy Type I (Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease Type 1A)", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Late-onset Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA Type 4)", "confidence": 0.62}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "Progressive arm and hand weakness with atrophy—sparring bulbar/respiratory function early—is highly suggestive of a lower motor neuron-predominant process. Limb-onset ALS is the most common cause of progressive asymmetric limb weakness with atrophy in adults; early sparing of bulbar/respiratory function is typical, hence high confidence (0.85). SMA Type 3 presents in adolescence/early adulthood with proximal > distal weakness and atrophy, often with preserved bulbar/respiratory function for decades—plausible but less common than ALS (0.78). Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (MMN) mimics ALS clinically but is treatable, typically shows conduction block on NCS, and spares bulbar/respiratory function—distinctive clinical pattern supports moderate-high confidence (0.72). CMT1A usually presents earlier (childhood/adolescence) with distal weakness and sensory involvement; pure motor presentation is rare, and atrophy is often accompanied by foot deformities and sensory loss—lower confidence due to lack of reported sensory symptoms or family history (0.65). SMA Type 4 has adult onset (>30 years), slow progression, and prominent limb-girdle distribution; isolated upper limb onset is less typical but possible—hence lowest confidence among top five (0.62). Excluded: Myasthenia gravis (bulbar/respiratory involvement common, fatigability not mentioned), inflammatory myopathies (proximal > distal, CK elevation expected), and cervical spondylotic myelopathy (usually includes spasticity, sensory signs, or reflex changes not described)."}

{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Multifocal Motor Neuropathy", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (limb-onset, early stage)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type III (Kugelberg-Welander)", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (motor-predominant variant)", "confidence": 0.65}, {"diagnosis": "Hereditary Motor and Sensory Neuropathy Type I (Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A) with atypical motor-predominant presentation", "confidence": 0.58}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "Progressive arm and hand weakness with atrophy—sparing bulbar/respiratory function early—strongly suggests a lower motor neuron or peripheral nerve disorder. Multifocal Motor Neuropathy (MMN) is top-ranked because it classically presents with asymmetric, progressive, purely motor limb weakness and atrophy, often with conduction block on NCS (a key diagnostic criterion the clinician explicitly asked about), and typically spares bulbar/respiratory function for years. ALS (limb-onset) remains highly plausible despite early bulbar sparing, as ~30% of cases present with isolated limb weakness and atrophy before spreading; however, its inclusion of upper motor neuron signs (not yet assessed) and eventual progression reduce confidence slightly relative to MMN. Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type III fits well: adult-onset, proximal > distal weakness, slow progression, and preserved bulbar/respiratory function until late stages—but lacks sensory involvement and shows symmetric atrophy, distinguishing it from MMN. CIDP (motor-predominant) is plausible but less likely without sensory symptoms or objective evidence of demyelination (e.g., prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction); its typical presentation includes some sensory involvement, lowering confidence. CMT1A is least likely in this context: though hereditary, it usually features prominent sensory loss, foot deformities, and distal > proximal weakness—motor-predominant variants are rare and often misdiagnosed; hence lowest confidence. Diagnostic uncertainty is moderate (entropy ~1.6), reflecting substantial overlap in early phenotypes and critical dependence on pending electrophysiological data (e.g., presence/absence of conduction block, EMG evidence of active denervation vs. chronic reinnervation, sensory nerve action potentials)."}
